title: Asilla's behavior-analysis AI at about 40 Japanese stations and buildings may have prompted two suicide interventions
summary: Kyodo (1 June 2026) reports Asilla's camera-analysis system at about 40 stations and buildings alerted guards in two cases where people later said they meant to jump; the claims are the developer's.
account: The date is the Kyodo report's publication as carried by The Straits Times; the two interventions are undated. Tokyo-based Asilla's system assesses the likelihood that a person will jump by analyzing behavior on security-camera footage. It looks for behavior such as pacing or lingering near a platform edge or rooftop. It alerts security guards and station staff, in some cases with loudspeaker warnings. In one case it detected a man loitering in a non-customer area of a commercial facility. A guard found him, and he later said he had intended to kill himself by jumping. In another, a child lingering near an upper-floor railing was found to have been writing a suicide note. Asilla says it trained the system since 2022 with around 200 facilities on about seven million pieces of footage. All details come from the company via Kyodo, and no operator, police or academic confirmation is among the sources. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor records the case.
purpose: Detect behavior indicating suicide risk (and illness, immobility or violence) in security-camera footage and alert staff.
